items.title: Oscar Peterson interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: We played, as you’d call them “eights” — challenges — eight bars for him, eight bars for me. And I’d play my eight bars, you know, and do my thing, and Basie would come up to his eight bars and he’d go like [brief scat] and wipe me out.

ctx.x: Well, I want to ask you about one other thing, too. I never forgot one thing. When I went in the studio in 1955 for Count Basie to record and I did “Every Day I have the Blues” and “Come Back” and the stuff that we did, Norman Granz, who sat in the control room and said, “ah, great, what else do you have for me?” That was his way of flattering me. “Oh that’s marvelous, what else do you have for me?” And then he turned to me and said, “remember where you made the first one,” you know. Now for me to go to Europe, I…

But that’s just one instance. In 1973 now, I’m sitting in a counter in Yugoslavia. I can’t even remember which city it was. Backstage. Because you know they have a place for artists to have a drink and some food backstage. But people from the theater can come back through a door and you can get into the theater through a door. And they were standing there with stacks of LP’s. And I signed each one. And Norman, sitting beside me right here at the bar, and I said, “you know you are very much responsible for this,…

items.title: Oscar Peterson interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: We used to do this Satch and Josh thing, with the two pianos... Norman said, 'and on the two pianos we have Oscar Peterson and Bill Basie'

ctx.x: I laugh because you told the story on yourself, somewhere I heard you telling the story on the air, you were playing and you got into some stride at the piano, and you were playing and you said you couldn’t get out of it, it just came, it just happened, and you happened to look in the wings, and there was Basie going —

That’s right. He brought a baseball bat. We used to do this Satch and Josh thing, with the two pianos. And one night he came out on the stage and Norman said, “and on the two pianos we have Oscar Peterson and Bill Basie, would you welcome them?” I walked up from this end and Basie walked from the other. He had a baseball bat.

For those of you who don’t quite understand, I must explain. You see, Basie and Oscar did a thing together. And the Satch — they told this story about Satchell Paige and Josh Gibson who was the greatest hitter I guess in baseball at the time, Negro baseball. He told Satchell Paige he said, “My mother and father are coming to watch me play. And at some point, Satchell, would you please let me hit one?” You know.

items.title: 52157_Count Basie oral history interview
items.q: seeing like Sweets Edison (inaudible) and Lockjaw Davis and (inaudible) and Oscar Peterson, [Zoot] and then being close to the old guys in Kansas City, some who I worked with and some I have been around with for many years

ctx.x: I had a few drops. It was real heavy and then getting the degree out at the university also, I mean, that was really -- but seeing all the guys, seeing like Sweets Edison (inaudible) and Lockjaw Davis and (inaudible) and Oscar Peterson, [Zoot] and then being close to the old guys in Kansas City, some who I worked with and some I have been around with for many years and (inaudible) Norman Granz who is the producer of [a man of] Pablo Capital Records who made it possible for Ella and Oscar and a couple of more…
